content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with 0.7 confidence. The evidence leans that way, but the noise was large, so it isn't conclusive.

**Design:** I trained the learner on L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested tasks grouped by how many of their rules were new, choosing them so that "how many rules are new" and "how similar to a trained task" pointed in different directions:

| New rules | Tasks tested | Mean examples to criterion | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (recombinations) | L1-S2-M3, L2-S3-M1, L3-S1-M2 | 20.5 | 16 |
| 1 | L1-S4-M1, L1-S1-M4, L4-S3-M3 | 24.1 | 16 |
| 2 | L4-S4-M1, L2-S4-M4 | 27.2 | 12 |
| 3 | L4-S4-M4 | 40.9 | 10 |

**Why part-based:**
- Cost went up steadily with each extra new rule.
- The recombinations were the cheapest group, even though each shares only one rule with any single trained task. The one-new-rule tasks share two rules with a trained task, and some also give the same responses on more inputs, yet they cost more.
- The two-new-rule tasks share the same amount with a trained task as the recombinations do, but they cost more. That fits "number of new rules" better than "similarity to a trained task".

**Why only 0.7:**
- Single tests varied a lot, from 1 to 68 examples (standard deviation about 15). Each comparison between adjacent groups is only marginally significant.
- The holistic learner's similarity measure is hidden. If it happens to track shared rules closely, it could produce a similar pattern.
- I had only three tests from before training (13, 22 and 52), so there is no reliable starting baseline.

**Process:** The sandbox blocked loops and scripts, so I ran each command separately. That is why I compared output overlap only for a few tasks instead of all 64. I miscounted the budget along the way: I planned 6 more tests on L4-S4-M1 and L2-S4-M4 than I had room for and was left with just 4. All 60 units are now spent and the session has ended.
